body.objective: Students will be able to read topographic maps.
successCriteria: I can read contour lines to understand land shape
I can use map scale to measure distance

body.hook: A topographic map is like a 3-D model squashed onto paper. With practice, you can look at a pattern of squiggly lines and "see" a valley, a cliff or a gentle hill, and plan the easiest route before you take a single step.

study.title: Reading the Land
study.question: How do topographic maps show the shape of the land?
study.passage:
Part 1, Fist mountain (10 minutes): Make a fist and use a washable marker to draw lines around your knuckles at the same height, as if water was rising. Open your fist and look from above: the lines show the shape of your "mountain."
Part 2, Contour rules (10 minutes):
• Lines close together = steep slope
• Lines far apart = gentle slope
• Circles inside circles = a hill or peak
• Lines making a V that points uphill = a valley or stream
• Contour lines never cross.
On a 1:50 000 Canadian topographic map, the contour interval is often 10 or 20 metres; check the legend.
Part 3, Scale (10 minutes): On a 1:50 000 map, 1 cm = 500 m, so 2 cm = 1 km. Use string to measure a winding trail, then convert to kilometres.
Part 4, Plan a route (15 minutes): Using a local topographic map (for example, a section of a provincial park), plan a route between two points. Find the distance, the total elevation gain and two landmarks. Choose a route that avoids the steepest slopes.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Canadian topographic map conventions from Natural Resources Canada.

body.objective: Students will be able to navigate with a compass.

successCriteria: I can identify the parts of a baseplate compass

body.hook: GPS can fail when batteries die or satellites drop out in a deep valley. A compass needs no power. Knowing how to take and follow a bearing is a skill that can get you home.

study.title: Finding Your Bearing
study.question: How do I navigate with a compass?
study.passage:
Compass skills (written for this lesson):
Parts: baseplate, direction-of-travel arrow, rotating housing (bezel) with degrees, orienting arrow, magnetic needle (red end points to magnetic north).
Cardinal bearings: N 0°/360°, E 90°, S 180°, W 270°.
Taking a bearing to an object: 1. Point the direction-of-travel arrow at the object. 2. Turn the housing until the orienting arrow lines up under the red needle ("red in the shed"). 3. Read the degrees at the index line.
Following a bearing: 1. Set the bearing on the housing. 2. Hold the compass flat in front of you. 3. Turn your whole body until red is in the shed. 4. Walk where the travel arrow points, picking a landmark on that line.
Declination: maps use true north; compasses point to magnetic north. In much of Alberta, magnetic north is roughly 13–15° east of true north and changes slowly over time; check the current value on your map or from Natural Resources Canada.
Activity: compass course on the field: follow three bearings and distances (using your pace length) to find a hidden marker.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; declination values are approximate and change over time.

body.objective: Students will be able to write a trip plan.
body.iCan: I can write a trip plan.
successCriteria: I can write a complete trip plan
I can identify hazards and plan for them
I can choose a route that fits the group's ability
body.hook: Many search-and-rescue calls begin the same way: nobody knew where the person went or when they'd be back. A trip plan left with someone at home is one of the simplest and most important safety tools.

vocabulary.definition: A written plan of where you're going, who's going, the route, timing and what to do if you're overdue.
The path you plan to travel.
Something that could cause harm, such as weather, water or wildlife.
A set time to head back no matter where you are.

study.title: Plan Before You Go
study.question: What goes into a safe trip plan?
study.passage:
Trip plan template (written for this lesson; based on common outdoor-safety guidance):
1. Who: names, ages, any medical conditions, emergency contacts.
2. Where: start point, route (attach a map with the route highlighted), destination, alternate routes.
3. When: departure time, turnaround time, expected return time, and the time the contact should call for help.
4. Gear: group and personal essentials, communication (charged phone; in remote areas, a satellite messenger).
5. Conditions: forecast, trail reports, wildlife advisories, fire bans (check Alberta Parks and Parks Canada sites).
6. Hazards and plans: e.g. thunderstorms → leave exposed ridges early; bears → travel in groups, make noise, carry bear spray (with trained adults); river crossings → avoid in high water.
7. Emergency plan: what the group does if someone is hurt or lost ("hug a tree": stay put and blow the whistle).
Activity: groups plan a 4–6 km day hike using a topographic map: calculate distance and elevation gain, estimate time (a common rule of thumb: about 4 km per hour plus extra time for climbing), set a turnaround time and fill the template.
